genxml.title: O2 CRIME memory controller and CPU interface registers
genxml.from: published CRIME 1.5 draft specification (rev 0.3), public Linux and NetBSD O2 drivers, and shipped IRIX software readings
genxml.doc: CRIME memory controller and CPU-interface registers, and the interrupt input bit positions.

struct.name: ID
struct.from: published CRIME 1.5 draft specification (rev 0.3), public Linux and NetBSD O2 drivers, and shipped IRIX software readings
struct.doc: The CPU interface registers, 0x14000000 to 0x14004048, take double-word accesses only (established, [spec] PDF 113). The same page asks, with a question mark, whether the memory control and rendering addresses follow that rule too, so the wider rule is unknown. Table 5-8 gives the 1.5 reset value as 0xb1, and its note gives the CRIME 1.1 ID as 0xa1 (established, [spec] PDF 114).

struct.name: INTSTAT
struct.from: published CRIME 1.5 draft specification (rev 0.3), public Linux and NetBSD O2 drivers, and shipped IRIX software readings
struct.doc: Read-only (established, [spec] Table 5-10, PDF 116). Each bit is the OR of the matching bit of the hardware interrupt register and of the software interrupt register (established, [spec] PDF 106).

struct.name: INTMASK
struct.from: published CRIME 1.5 draft specification (rev 0.3), public Linux and NetBSD O2 drivers, and shipped IRIX software readings
struct.doc: A status bit reaches the processor only when the same bit here is set. The status register is ANDed with this one, bit for bit, to make the interrupts (established, [spec] PDF 106 and PDF 233). Table 5-11 (PDF 117) gives bits 31:0 as read/write, 1 enabling, reset zero. It has no row for bits 63:32, so their effect on the hardware is unknown.

struct.name: SOFTINT

struct.name: HARDINT
struct.from: published CRIME 1.5 draft specification (rev 0.3), public Linux and NetBSD O2 drivers, and shipped IRIX software readings
struct.doc: Table 5-13 (PDF 117 to 118) marks these bits edge-sensitive: 30 (CPU SysCorErr), 24 to 22 (rendering idle, full and empty) and 19 to 16 (GBE). It marks 27 to 25 (rendering idle, full and empty levels) level-sensitive. The table leaves the other status bits unlabelled (established).

struct.name: TIMER
struct.from: published CRIME 1.5 draft specification (rev 0.3), public Linux and NetBSD O2 drivers, and shipped IRIX software readings
struct.doc: Free-running counter. The specification defines bits 31:0 as read/write with reset zero and gives no field above bit 31 (established, [spec] PDF 113 places it at offset 0x38 and Table 5-15 on PDF 119 defines the low 32 bits). The same page gives a nominal rate of about 66.7 MHz (established as spec prose; not an oscillator measurement). NetBSD's crime header masks 48 bits, so the width above bit 31 is open (see docs/open-questions.md). The low word would sit at offset 0x3c under big-endian addressing, and IRIX's query_cyclecntr returns 0xb400003c as the address of the counter's low word (software expectation, so inferred; docs/functions.md). Whether a four-byte read there returns the same count is unknown. The CPU-interface rule allows doubleword accesses only (established, [spec] PDF 113), and Table 5-1 (printed page 5-5, PDF 93) lists single and partial-word processor requests without saying whether they reach these registers (see docs/open-questions.md).

struct.name: CPU_ERROR_ADDR
struct.from: published CRIME 1.5 draft specification (rev 0.3), public Linux and NetBSD O2 drivers, and shipped IRIX software readings
struct.doc: Records address bits 33:2 of a failed CPU programmed-I/O access, in the low 32 bits (established, [spec] Table 5-16, PDF 120). The spec records it for a SysAD parity error or an invalid address. Whether clearing the status also clears this register or the interrupt cause is unknown. The spec says software would like bits 39:34 captured as well (established, [spec] PDF 233); see the status register.

struct.name: CPU_ERROR_STAT
struct.from: published CRIME 1.5 draft specification (rev 0.3), public Linux and NetBSD O2 drivers, and shipped IRIX software readings
struct.doc: Set by hardware, cleared by software (established, [spec] Table 5-17, PDF 120). This is the CRIME 1.1 offset; the 1.5 specification gives the register's address as 0x14004048 (see cpu_error_stat_15). Bits 1 and 0 are no longer supported on 1.5 because SysADC is not used (established, PDF 120). Bits 8:3 hold address bits 39:34 on 1.5 "if it can be implemented"; whether fitted parts do is unknown. The spec does not define "invalid address", so whether a refused CPU access sets bit 2 is unknown.

struct.name: CPU_ERROR_ENA
struct.from: published CRIME 1.5 draft specification (rev 0.3), public Linux and NetBSD O2 drivers, and shipped IRIX software readings
struct.doc: The CRIME 1.5 CPU interface register map has no row for this offset. It lists the CPU error address and the CPU error status (cpu_error_stat_15) and nothing in between (established, [spec] Table 5-7, PDF 113). The name CRIME_CPU_ERROR_ENA and this offset come from NetBSD's public crime header, which places it after the CPU error status. The driver in that tree does not program the name (software expectation, inferred). Linux's public O2 crime header leaves the same slot as padding after the status (software expectation, inferred). Reset value, field layout and readback are unknown from any published source; the revision-0 enable word that IRIX writes is described in docs/memory.md.

struct.name: MEM_BANK_CONTROL
struct.from: published CRIME 1.5 draft specification (rev 0.3), public Linux and NetBSD O2 drivers, and shipped IRIX software readings
struct.doc: Bits 7:5 are reserved and read as zero (established, [spec] PDF 150 and 152, CRIME 1.5 specification rev 0.3).

struct.name: MEM_ERROR_STAT
struct.from: published CRIME 1.5 draft specification (rev 0.3), public Linux and NetBSD O2 drivers, and shipped IRIX software readings
struct.doc:
Reset values differ per bank, so the REG line's reset=unknown stands for none of them: bank n resets to n for n = 0 to 7 (established, [spec] table 6-14; no shipped software writes banks 2 to 7). With 32 MiB parts that puts bank n at n * 32 MiB. #define CRIME_MEM_BANK_CONTROL_RESET_BASE 0 /* established: reset of bank 0 #define CRIME_MEM_BANK_CONTROL_RESET_STEP 1 /* established: reset of bank n is BASE + n * STEP
The shipped IRIX kernel's address probes write zero here before each probe, then check that causes 20 and 21 read clear (software expectation, inferred). Whether a zero write clears the latch on the part is unknown: the specification's clear polarity for this register is not established (PDF 152 to 155, unread here).

struct.name: MEM_ERROR_ECC_REPL
struct.from: published CRIME 1.5 draft specification (rev 0.3), public Linux and NetBSD O2 drivers, and shipped IRIX software readings
struct.doc: The published table defines only bits 7:0 and gives reset zero (established, [spec] Table 6-20, PDF 155). The full-width mask 0xffffffff in Linux's public crime header does not establish 32 independent replacement bits; it conflicts with that table (software expectation, inferred). Readback of bits 63:8 is unspecified (unknown).

struct.name: CPU_ERROR_STAT_15
struct.from: published CRIME 1.5 draft specification (rev 0.3), public Linux and NetBSD O2 drivers, and shipped IRIX software readings
struct.doc: The CRIME 1.5 specification places the CPU error status register here, on its own 16 KiB page so that it can be mapped to user programs (established, [spec] Table 5-7 and its note, PDF 113). Bit layout as in Table 5-17 (PDF 120). The grade stays inferred: whether a fitted part implements this offset is not established.

struct.name: INTBIT
struct.from: published CRIME 1.5 draft specification (rev 0.3), public Linux and NetBSD O2 drivers, and shipped IRIX software readings
struct.doc: Interrupt status bit positions, from the CRIME 1.5 specification's Table 5-5 (PDF 106 to 108; established). Each bit is ORed with others onto one R10000 interrupt line, IP2 to IP6, given by the CRIME_IP*_CAUSES constants. CRIME signals the processor when a bit in a group asserts or de-asserts (established, PDF 106). Table 5-6 (PDF 109) pairs IP2 to IP6 with cause register bits 10 to 14 and SysAD bits 0 to 4. The prose on PDF 109 and PDF 110 swaps bits 20 and 21. Table 5-5, Table 5-10 (PDF 116) and the revision note on PDF 233 do not, so bit 20 is the CPU interface error and bit 21 the memory error (established).
